```

The regression model demonstrate that burning restrictions and burning costs have the greatest difference in impact on forager mobility (Figure S\@ref(fig:fm-mm-regs_3). Stricter limits on burning behaviors and higher costs result in higher levels of mobility over the course of model run. Interestingly, the predicted amount of mobility for the highest burning cost shows an increase in average moves per foraging bout. This pattern is impossible in the model because we cap mobility at a maximum value. The contrast of this with the other burning costs demonstrates the differential impact that low cost niche construction strategies can have on forager behaviors.

## Correlations between mobility and distributions of vegetation types

These mobility patterns due to different limits on burning behaviors occur because burning controls the energy available in the environment such that less burning means less overall energy, so agents need to move further to meet their energy needs.

```{r mobility-veg-correlations, fig.cap="Correlations between forager mobility (mean.fm), vegetation diversity (shannon.div), vegetation spatial autocorrelation (veg_morans.i), and high value vegetation types (veg_7, veg_6, veg_5) at beginning, middle, and end of model run from left to right", echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, out.width='100%'}
par(mfrow = c(1,3))
par(mar=c(0,1,0,1))
#plot at 250
pvalue250 = psych::corr.test(data250 %>% 
                               select(mean.fm, shannon.div, 
                                      veg_morans.i, veg_7, veg_6, veg_5))$p
corrplot::corrplot(cor(data250 %>% 
                         select(mean.fm, shannon.div, 
                                veg_morans.i, veg_7, veg_6, veg_5), 
                       use = "pairwise.complete.obs"),
                   method = "square", 
                   addCoef.col = "black", 
                   col = scales::alpha(corrplot::COL2("RdBu"), alpha = 0.85),
                   p.mat = pvalue250, 
                   insig="blank", 
                   sig.level=0.1, 
                   type = "lower", 
                   number.cex = 0.5, 
                   diag=F)

#plot at 2000
pvalue2000 = psych::corr.test(data2000 %>% 
                                select(mean.fm, shannon.div, 
                                       veg_morans.i, veg_7, veg_6, veg_5))$p
corrplot::corrplot(cor(data2000 %>% 
                         select(mean.fm, shannon.div, 
                                veg_morans.i, veg_7, veg_6, veg_5), 
                       use = "pairwise.complete.obs"),
                   method = "square", 
                   addCoef.col = "black", 
                   col = scales::alpha(corrplot::COL2("RdBu"), alpha = 0.85),
                   p.mat = pvalue2000, 
                   insig="blank", 
                   sig.level=0.1, 
                   type = "lower", 
                   number.cex = 0.5, 
                   diag=F)

#plot at 3500
pvalue3500 = psych::corr.test(data3500 %>% 
                                select(mean.fm, shannon.div, 
                                       veg_morans.i, veg_7, veg_6, veg_5))$p
corrplot::corrplot(cor(data3500 %>% 
                         select(mean.fm, shannon.div, 
                                veg_morans.i, veg_7, veg_6, veg_5), 
                       use = "pairwise.complete.obs"),
                   method = "square", 
                   addCoef.col = "black", 
                   col = scales::alpha(corrplot::COL2("RdBu"), alpha = 0.85),
                   p.mat = pvalue3500, 
                   insig="blank", 
                   sig.level=0.1, 
                   type = "lower", 
                   number.cex = 0.5, 
                   diag=F)

```

We can see this pattern exemplified when looking at correlations between forager movement (*mean.fm*) and the highest vegetation types (*veg_7*, *veg_6*, *veg_5*), that is those that provide the most resources. We generally see negative correlations with the high vegetation types (Figure S\@ref(fig:mobility-veg-correlations)), indicating that low forager mobility is significantly correlated with higher proportions of these vegetation types. 

We can also see that low forager mobility is highly correlated with dispersion of vegetation types, as is evidenced by the positive correlation between *mean.fm* and *veg_morans.i*. This indicates that local heterogeneity of the landscape affects how far the foragers need to move. 

## Correlations between forager mobility and population density

Because mobility is the behavior that agents can control in the model, we looked at how changes in this behavior changes with population evolution. 

```{r mobility-pop-correlations_1, fig.cap="Relationship between average steps per foraging bout during climatic intervals and the resulting population density during the same climatic interval for model scenarios with short climatic cycles (100 ticks)", echo=FALSE, fig.height=8, fig.width=8, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, out.width='100%'}
ggplot(rates %>% 
         filter(`veg-cycle-start` == "\"productive\"") %>% 
         filter(`cycle-duration` == "100") %>%
         filter(`movement-model` == "\"Directed Walk\"")) +
  geom_point(aes(y = end.pop.density, x = start.steps, 
                 color = climate.condition)) +
  geom_smooth(aes(y = end.pop.density, x = start.steps), 
              method = "lm") +
  stat_cor(mapping = aes(y = end.pop.density, x = start.steps), 
           method = "pearson", p.accuracy = 0.01, r.accuracy = 0.01, 
           size = 2.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ tick.range, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 6), 
        legend.position = "bottom", 
        strip.text = element_text(size = 7))

```

Because there is relatively little change in forager steps within climatic intervals, we looked at the relationship between the starting number of steps during a climatic interval and the resulting population density at the end of that interval. Throughout model run, these outputs are highly negatively correlated (Figure S\@ref(fig:mobility-pop-correlations_1)). This suggests that lower amounts of mobility lead to higher population densities because each foraging group requires less room to meet their foraging needs.

# Forager interactions

When looking at forager interactions, we have to consider them in relation to populations since more foragers on the landscape will necessarily mean more possible interactions. The model outputs interaction counts averaged across all agents and we divided this by the population count to get the average proportion of the population that an individual agent interacts with each tick.

```{r adj-fi-viz, fig.cap="Trends in average proportion of population a given agent interacts with across model run", echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.height=7}
ggplot(data %>% filter(ticks > 0)) +
  geom_smooth(aes(x = ticks, y = adj.fi, color = `movement-model`), se = T) +
  facet_grid(`cycle-duration` + `veg-cycle-start` ~ `burn-cost`, 
             labeller = labeller(`veg-cycle-start` = start.labs, 
                                 `cycle-duration` = cycle.labs, 
                                 `burn-cost` = bc.labs)) +
  scale_color_colorblind() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", strip.text = element_text(size = 6))

```

When we visualize these differences (Figure S\@ref(fig:adj-fi-viz)), we can see that for random walks, there is a steep drop off in forager interactions within approximately the first 500 ticks of the model. This is likely because populations are relatively small at the beginning of model run, so each interaction will necessarily be a greater proportion. For the subsequent analyses, we look at the patterns occurring after the first 500 ticks to understand how the parameters affect interactions after a larger population has been established. 

```{r adj-fi-reg_1, fig.cap="Standardized regression coefficients for effect of model parameters and their interaction with time on average proportion of population foragers interact with across model run", echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, out.width='100%', fig.height=5}
fi.data = data %>% filter(ticks > 500)

#plotNormalDensity(fi.data$adj.fi)

parameters = c(
  "cycle-duration",  # 100, 250
  "veg-cycle-start", # productive, unproductive
  "veg-distribution", # random, clustered
  "burnt-neighbor-limit", # 1, 4, 8
  "burn-cost", # 0, 50
  "burn-veg-type-threshold", # 4, 7
  "movement-model" #Random, Directed
)

fi.fit1 = lm(adj.fi ~ ticks*(.), data = fi.data %>% 
               dplyr::select_at(c(parameters, "ticks", "adj.fi")))

plot_summs(fi.fit1, scale = T)

```

By comparing standardized regression coefficients (Figure S\@ref(fig:adj-fi-reg_1)), we can see the greatest effect on forager interactions is movement models and burn cost. Because the shape of the trend lines is different enough between random walks and directed walks, we split the data by movement model to further investigate parameter effects.

```{r adj-fi-reg_2, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, out.width='100%', fig.height=3}
rw.data = fi.data %>% filter(`movement-model` == "\"Random Walk\"") 
dw.data = fi.data %>% filter(`movement-model` == "\"Directed Walk\"") 

dw.fit1 = lm(adj.fi ~ ticks*(.), data = dw.data %>% 
               filter(ticks > 0) %>% 
               select_at(c("ticks", "adj.fi", parameters[-7])))

rw.fit1 = lm(adj.fi ~ ticks*(.), data = rw.data %>% 
               filter(ticks > 0) %>% 
               select_at(c("ticks", "adj.fi", parameters[-7])))

par(mfrow = c(1,2))
par(mar=c(1,1,1,1))
plot(dw.fit1, which = 2)
plot(rw.fit1, which = 2)

```

The QQ plots show relatively good model performance.

```{r parameter-effects-adj-fi_1, fig.cap="Standardized regression coefficients for effect of model parameters and their interaction with time on average proportion of population foragers interact with across model run split by movement model",  out.width="100%", echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.height = 4}

plot_summs(dw.fit1, rw.fit1, scale = T, 
           model.names = c("directed walks", "random walks"))

```

```{r parameter-effects-adj-fi_2, fig.cap="Predicted proportions of populations foragers interact with across model run for different burn costs and movement models", out.width="100%", echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.height = 4}

ggarrange(
  ggeffects::ggpredict(dw.fit1, terms = c("ticks", "burn-cost")) %>%
    plot(show_data = FALSE, show_ci = FALSE, limits = c(0, 0.020)) +
    theme(title = element_text(size = 7)), 
  ggeffects::ggpredict(rw.fit1, terms = c("ticks", "burn-cost")) %>%
    plot(show_data = FALSE, show_ci = FALSE, limits = c(0, 0.020)) +
    theme(title = element_text(size = 7)),
  common.legend = T, legend = "bottom", 
  labels = c("Directed Walk", "Random Walk"), 
  nrow = 1, ncol = 2, 
  font.label = list(size = 8), vjust = 0.8
) +
  theme(plot.margin = margin(0.1,0.2,0.1,0.1, "cm"), 
        title = element_text(size = 7))

```

These two regressions demonstrate that restrictions/costs to burning behaviors impact forager interactions, but that these effects are much more prominent and diverging for directed walks (Figures S\@ref(fig:parameter-effects-adj-fi_1) & S\@ref(fig:parameter-effects-adj-fi_2)). This again indicates that the amount of burning has a significant impact on the evolution of human behaviors in the model. 

## Change in forager interactions over time
```{r interaction-change-over-time, fig.cap="Change in proportion of the population foragers interact with across each climatic interval", out.width="100%", fig.height=6, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
ggplot(rates %>% 
         filter(`veg-cycle-start` == "\"productive\"") %>% 
         filter(`cycle-duration` == "250")) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x = tick.range, y = interactions.slope, 
                   color = climate.condition)) +
  facet_grid( `movement-model` ~ `burn-cost`, 
              scales = "free", labeller = label_both) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = 0), color = "black") +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, size = 6), 
        legend.position = 'bottom')

```
As is expected, when we look at how forager interactions changes over across climate intervals, there is very limited change except in the earliest intervals during which populations are being established. When changes does occur, it is primarily with agents performing directed walks and when burning costs are lower (Figure S\@ref(fig:interaction-change-over-time). 

## Relationship between forager interactions and: forager mobility and population density
Therefore, we investigate how interaction rates over time are related to mobility and population density only with directed walks. 
```{r interactions-mobility, fig.cap="Relationship between proportion of population foragers interact with and steps per foraging bout at the beginning of each climatic interval across model run", echo=FALSE, fig.height=8, fig.width=8, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, out.width="100%"}
ggplot(rates %>% 
         filter(`veg-cycle-start` == "\"productive\"") %>% 
         filter(`cycle-duration` == "100") %>% 
         filter(`movement-model` == "\"Directed Walk\"")) +
  geom_point(aes(y = start.steps, x = start.interactions, 
                 color = climate.condition)) +
  geom_smooth(aes(y = start.steps, x = start.interactions), 
              method = "lm") +
  stat_cor(mapping = aes(y = start.steps, x = start.interactions), 
           method = "pearson", p.accuracy = 0.01, r.accuracy = 0.01, 
           size = 2.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ tick.range, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 6), 
        legend.position = "bottom", 
        strip.text = element_text(size = 7))

```
Interactions are highly positively correlated with mobility throughout model run (Figure S\@ref(fig:interactions-mobility)), meaning that more mobility allows for more interactions with directed walks. 

```{r interactions-mobility_2, fig.cap="Relationship between proportion of the population foragers interact with and number of steps per foraging bout for a climatic period at the middle of model run. Relationship visualized by model scenarios with different burning costs", echo=FALSE, fig.height=6, fig.width=8, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, out.width="100%"}
ggplot(rates %>% filter(`veg-cycle-start` == "\"productive\"") %>% 
         filter(`cycle-duration` == "100") %>% 
         filter(`movement-model` == "\"Directed Walk\"") %>%
         filter(tick.range == "1001-1100")) +
  geom_point(aes(y = start.steps, x = start.interactions, 
                 color = climate.condition)) +
  geom_smooth(aes(y = start.steps, x = start.interactions), 
              method = "lm") +
  stat_cor(mapping = aes(y = start.steps, x = start.interactions), 
           method = "pearson", p.accuracy = 0.01, r.accuracy = 0.01, 
           size = 4) +
  facet_wrap(~ `burn-cost`, scales = "free_x", labeller = label_both) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 6), legend.position = "bottom")

```

The strength of these correlations is impacted by burning costs. For example, if we take a productive climate interval in the middle of model run (Figure S\@ref(fig:interactions-mobility_2)), we see significant and stronger correlations only when burning costs are low, so when burning is more frequent. 

```{r interactions-population, fig.cap="Relationship between proportion of the population foragers interact with and population density for a climatic period at the middle of model run. Relationship visualized by model scenarios with different burning costs", echo=FALSE, fig.height=6, fig.width=8, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, out.width="100%"}
ggplot(rates %>% filter(`veg-cycle-start` == "\"productive\"") %>% 
         filter(`cycle-duration` == "100") %>% 
         filter(`movement-model` == "\"Directed Walk\"") %>%
         filter(tick.range == "1001-1100")) +
  geom_point(aes(y = start.pop.density, x = start.interactions, 
                 color = climate.condition)) +
  geom_smooth(aes(y = start.pop.density, x = start.interactions), 
              method = "lm") +
  stat_cor(mapping = aes(y = start.pop.density, x = start.interactions), 
           method = "pearson", p.accuracy = 0.01, r.accuracy = 0.01, 
           size = 4) +
  facet_wrap(~ `burn-cost`, scales = "free_x", labeller = label_both) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 6), legend.position = "bottom")
```
The same is true for negative correlations between interactions and population density, although here the strongest relationship is when there is no burning cost (Figure S\@ref(fig:interactions-population)). 

These results are because there is minimal change in forager mobility and therefore interactions at the highest burning costs. 

## Maintaining connections with the same foragers
In addition to understanding overall forager interaction rates, we also loosely investigated the formation of social networks. To do so, we tracked how many of a forager's interactions during a given foraging bout overlapped with the interactions of the previous bout. Doing this provides insight into whether foragers are consistently interacting with new people or if there is incipient formation of social groups. If social groups were "forming", we would expect to see increased proportions of interactions being comprised of the same foragers. 

```{r same-network_1, fig.cap="Trends in average proportion of interactions that are the same as the previous tick across model run. Trend lines are shown for each individual climatic interval. Results shown for model scenarios with long climatic cycles (250 ticks)", echo=FALSE, fig.height=5, fig.width=8, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

plot.data3$`burn-cost` =  as.factor(plot.data3$`burn-cost`)

  # geom_smooth(data = plot.data3, 
  #             mapping = aes(x = ticks, y = same.fi.prop, color = `burn-cost`)) +
  geom_smooth(data = plot.data3 %>% filter(ticks > 0 & ticks <= 250), 
              mapping = aes(x = ticks, y = same.fi.prop, 
                            color = climate.condition), 
              method = "lm") +
  geom_smooth(data = plot.data3 %>% filter(ticks > 250 & ticks <= 500), 
              mapping = aes(x = ticks, y = same.fi.prop, 
                            color = climate.condition), 
              method = "lm") +
  geom_smooth(data = plot.data3 %>% filter(ticks > 500 & ticks <= 750), 
              mapping = aes(x = ticks, y = same.fi.prop, 
                            color = climate.condition), 
              method = "lm") +
  geom_smooth(data = plot.data3 %>% filter(ticks > 750 & ticks <= 1000), 
              mapping = aes(x = ticks, y = same.fi.prop, 
                            color = climate.condition), 
              method = "lm") +
  geom_smooth(data = plot.data3 %>% filter(ticks > 1000 & ticks <= 1250), 
              mapping = aes(x = ticks, y = same.fi.prop, 
                            color = climate.condition), 
              method = "lm") +
  geom_smooth(data = plot.data3 %>% filter(ticks > 1250 & ticks <= 1500), 
              mapping = aes(x = ticks, y = same.fi.prop, 
                            color = climate.condition), 
              method = "lm") +
  geom_smooth(data = plot.data3 %>% filter(ticks > 1500 & ticks <= 1750), 
              mapping = aes(x = ticks, y = same.fi.prop, 
                            color = climate.condition), 
              method = "lm") +
  geom_smooth(data = plot.data3 %>% filter(ticks > 1750 & ticks <= 2000), 
              mapping = aes(x = ticks, y = same.fi.prop, 
                            color = climate.condition), 
              method = "lm") +
  geom_smooth(data = plot.data3 %>% filter(ticks > 2000 & ticks <= 2250), 
              mapping = aes(x = ticks, y = same.fi.prop, 
                            color = climate.condition), 
              method = "lm") +
  geom_smooth(data = plot.data3 %>% filter(ticks > 2250 & ticks <= 2500), 
              mapping = aes(x = ticks, y = same.fi.prop, 
                            color = climate.condition), 
              method = "lm") +
  geom_smooth(data = plot.data3 %>% filter(ticks > 2500 & ticks <= 2750), 
              mapping = aes(x = ticks, y = same.fi.prop, 
                            color = climate.condition), 
              method = "lm") +
  geom_smooth(data = plot.data3 %>% filter(ticks > 2750 & ticks <= 3000), 
              mapping = aes(x = ticks, y = same.fi.prop, 
                            color = climate.condition), 
              method = "lm") +
  geom_smooth(data = plot.data3 %>% filter(ticks > 3000 & ticks <= 3250), 
              mapping = aes(x = ticks, y = same.fi.prop, 
                            color = climate.condition), 
              method = "lm") +
  geom_smooth(data = plot.data3 %>% filter(ticks > 3250 & ticks <= 3500), 
              mapping = aes(x = ticks, y = same.fi.prop, 
                            color = climate.condition),

  #geom_vline(aes(xintercept = 2500), color = "black") +

  labs(y = "average same interaction proportion")

```

When we plot the change in average proportion of interactions that are the same as the previous tick across model run by burn cost and movement model, we see that random walks result in overall higher proportions of agents interacting with the same people compared to directed walks (Figure S\@ref(fig:same-network_1)). This is driven primarily by high rates of similar interactions in unproductive periods, particularly when burning costs are high. 

Conversely, with directed walks, we see an initial dip in the proportion of interactions that are with the same people as the population is establishing itself. This makes sense because the population is relatively unstable at this time, so there will be more new people on the landscape. 

If we consider after that burn in period, we see that the proportion of interactions that are with the same people starts to increase again and remains higher as the population reaches equilibrium and carrying capacity (Figure S\@ref(fig:same-network_1)). Because directed walks also result in fewer interactions over the course of model run, this suggests that directed walks in landscapes with a long history of burning and stable population result in smaller social networks, with foragers frequently interacting with the same people.
